title: Responsible AI
body: Practice of developing AI systems that are transparent, fair, accountable, and aligned with human values. Includes explainability, bias detection, privacy protection, and compliance. Critical in regulated industries like insurance.

title: Model Explainability
body: Making model predictions understandable to humans. Includes explaining individual predictions (LIME, SHAP) and global patterns (feature importance). Required by regulations for high-stakes decisions.

title: Fairness (in ML) / Model Fairness
body: Ensuring model predictions don't systematically disadvantage specific groups. Measured via fairness metrics (demographic parity, equalized odds). Essential in insurance underwriting and lending.

title: Bias Detection
body: Methods for identifying systematic errors where models unfairly favor or disfavor certain groups. Tools like Fairness-indicators, AI Fairness 360 detect bias across demographics.

metadata.source: Google Fairness Indicators, IBM AI Fairness 360

title: Disparate Impact
body: Legal concept where policies or decisions have a disproportionate negative effect on protected groups, even if not intentionally discriminatory. Models can cause disparate impact; must be audited and mitigated.

title: AI Governance
body: Framework for overseeing AI systems across an organization: model approval workflows, risk assessment, compliance monitoring, incident handling. Databricks and other platforms provide governance tooling.

title: Model Governance
body: Policies and processes for managing model lifecycle: registration, validation, approval, deployment, monitoring, retirement. Ensures only validated models reach production.

title: Data Privacy / Privacy-Preserving ML
body: Protecting sensitive personal data (PII) throughout ML pipeline. Techniques: data minimization, PII masking, differential privacy, federated learning. Regulated by GDPR, CCPA, and industry standards.

title: PII (Personally Identifiable Information) Masking
body: Removing or anonymizing sensitive identifiers (names, emails, social security numbers) in data. Essential in financial/insurance systems. Can be done via hashing, tokenization, or synthetic data generation.

title: Differential Privacy
body: Mathematical framework ensuring that removing any individual's data from analysis doesn't significantly change results. Enables sharing insights without leaking personal data. Growing use in public datasets.

title: Federated Learning
body: Training ML models across distributed data without centralizing sensitive data. Participants train locally, share model updates (not raw data) with central server. Preserves privacy and security.

title: Model Audit / AI Audit
body: Formal review of model design, data, training process, and deployment for bias, fairness, safety, and compliance. Identifies risks and documents findings for regulatory submission.

title: Transparency / Transparency in AI
body: Making AI systems' decisions understandable and observable. Includes documentation (what data, algorithms, design choices), explainability (why predictions made), and audit trails (who accessed what).

title: Accountability
body: Clear assignment of responsibility for AI system decisions and outcomes. Includes audit trails, escalation paths, and ability to reverse or explain decisions. Essential for regulated systems.

title: Audit Trail / Model Provenance
body: Complete record of model's history: who trained it, when, with what data/code, evaluation results, deployment decisions. Enables compliance verification and root-cause analysis.

title: Regulatory Compliance / Compliance in AI
body: Ensuring AI systems meet legal and industry regulations. Examples: GDPR (EU data protection), fair lending laws (USA), insurance regulatory requirements. Achieved through explainability, bias testing, and documentation.

title: GDPR (General Data Protection Regulation)
body: EU regulation protecting personal data privacy. Key requirements: consent, data minimization, right to deletion, breach notification, data portability. Impacts any organization processing EU residents' data.

title: Model Risk Management
body: Framework for identifying, measuring, and managing risks posed by AI/ML models in production. Includes validation (before deployment), monitoring (ongoing), and incident response (when issues detected).

title: Model Validation
body: Testing models before deployment: backtesting on historical data, stress testing on edge cases, bias validation, fairness audits. Ensures models meet business and compliance requirements.

title: Backtesting
body: Testing a model's historical performance by running it on past data it wasn't trained on. Validates model accuracy and identifies periods of degradation. Critical for financial/insurance models.

title: Model Stress Testing
body: Testing models on extreme, adversarial, or unusual inputs to find failure modes. Identifies edge cases, robustness issues, and potential harms. Required before high-stakes deployments.

title: Adversarial Examples / Adversarial Robustness
body: Inputs crafted to fool models into making incorrect predictions. Testing against adversarial examples ensures robustness. Important for security-critical applications (fraud detection).

title: Model Debugging
body: Investigating model errors and unexpected behavior to understand root causes. Tools: SHAP (identify problematic features), error analysis (group errors by pattern), data inspection (check training data).

title: Model Reproducibility
body: Ability to recreate exact model training run and results given same data/code/parameters. Achieved via version control, dependency pinning, random seeds, and experiment tracking.

title: Model Documentation
body: Recording model design decisions, data used, assumptions, limitations, and known issues. Model cards (Google) and datasheets (Timnit Gebru) are standardized formats.

title: Model Card
body: Standardized one-pager documenting model: purpose, intended use, training data, performance metrics, bias/fairness evaluation, limitations, recommendations. Promotes transparency and accountability.

title: Datasheet for Datasets
body: Documentation standard for datasets including: motivation (why created), composition (what data), collection process, labeling process, uses, limitations, and maintenance plan.

title: Interpretability vs Accuracy Trade-off
body: Complex models (deep learning) achieve higher accuracy but lower interpretability. Simple models (decision trees) are more interpretable but less accurate. Domain and use case determine acceptable trade-off.
